newsitem.title: ROMANIA: IMF mission to assess Romania progress.
newsitem.headline: IMF mission to assess Romania progress.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund mission visits Romania next week to assess progress in implementing reforms and release the next instalment of a stand-by credit, the Fund's Bucharest mission said on Friday.
"They are coming to discuss with the government the first review of the programme for the first half of the year under the IMF stand-by," resident representative John Hill said by telephone.
Benchmarks and performance criteria for the rest of the year will also be agreed. A second review is due early in 1998.

The IMF approved credits of $430 million for Romania in April after agreeing on reform targets with the centrist government. A first installment of about $86 million under the 13-month stand-by loan was made available immediately.

"If the mission determines that the performance criteria were met and once the first review is completed, Romania will be eligible for the next disbursement," Hill said. "The board will be concluding the first review in September or October."
All five tranches are of about equal value.

The main objectives of the reform programme were to reduce monthly inflation to about two percent in the second half of 1997, cut the current account deficit to $1.4 billion from last year's $2.3 billion and increase foreign exchange reserves.
Inflation last month was 2.3 percent, down from a 30.7 percent blip in March after Romania liberalised prices for staples and energy prices.
The central bank's foreign exchange reserves climbed to $1.996 billion at end-June from $1.495 billion the previous month. They are expected to hit $3 billion by end-1997.
Plans call for the budget deficit to be trimmed to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product from 5.8 percent in 1996.

Romania's reformist government, which took power last November after seven years of leftist rule, has been scrambling to meet reform targets and secure the confidence of Western lenders and investors.

It rammed an austerity budget through parliament in record time and secured approval of bank privatisation and foreign owenership of land. It presented new foreign investment rules and announced faster privatisation and restructuring targets.
The IMF suspended credits last year, saying the leftist government of the time had overspent and hobbled foreign exchange markets ahead of the election it eventually lost.

The World Bank, which also withheld loans last year, approved $550 million in a credit package to Romania in May to help restructure the farming sector, upgrade infrastructure and cushion the effects of reforms.
